posts.text:
On the night of March 29, 1993, Jack Palance opened the envelope for Best Supporting Actress and read the name out loud.

Marisa Tomei.

There was a gasp in the room. Not the usual intake of breath that follows a surprising announcement — something more confused than that, more searching. People in the audience turned to each other. The camera found her face. She walked to the stage.

She gave her speech. She held the Oscar. She went home.

The rumour started almost immediately.

She hadn’t really won. Jack Palance had read the wrong name. He was old. He was confused. He was reading from the teleprompter instead of the envelope. The wrong woman had walked away with the statue, and the Academy — too embarrassed to admit it — had simply let it happen.

The story spread. Film critics printed it. Dinner parties repeated it. It became one of those facts that lived in the space between rumour and certainty, repeated with enough confidence that no one stopped to check. 

The Academy issued statements. The accountants who count the ballots issued statements. It had all been correct, they said. She had won. The name on the card was hers.

None of this stopped anyone.

Here is what had actually happened, and why it unsettled people enough to invent an explanation.

She had grown up in Brooklyn, the daughter of a teacher and a lawyer. She went to high school in the same neighbourhood where she was born, then to Boston University, which she left before finishing to do what she had always wanted to do. Soap operas first — a recurring role on As the World Turns. Then television, a part on A Different World. Then smaller film roles, the kind that don’t change careers.

My Cousin Vinny arrived in 1992. It was a courtroom comedy about a New York lawyer defending his cousin on a murder charge in rural Alabama. Marisa Tomei played Mona Lisa Vito — Vinny’s fiancée from Brooklyn, all manicured nails and borrowed confidence and the iron certainty that the people around her were simply not keeping up.

The film had a courtroom scene near the end. Vinny calls Mona Lisa as an expert witness on automotive mechanics. She proceeds, in a cocktail dress, to dismantle the prosecution’s theory of the crime with detailed, specific, entirely accurate expertise about the 1964 Buick Skylark. The scene turns on the gap between how she looks and what she knows — and on the audience realising, along with the defence attorney, that she has known it all along.

It was a perfect scene. It remains a perfect scene.

The Academy gave her the Oscar for it.

And this, apparently, was the problem. She had played a funny woman from Brooklyn. The other nominees had appeared in Howards End and Damage and Enchanted April — serious films, serious roles, the kind the Academy was supposed to reward. Film critic Rex Reed suggested publicly that a mistake had been made. The Hollywood Reporter ran the rumour. The story found legs because it already fit something people believed: that a comedic performance couldn’t really be that good, that an unknown from Brooklyn couldn’t really have beaten Vanessa Redgrave, that something must have gone wrong.

What actually went wrong was that the room had decided what she was before she opened her mouth.

The years that followed were not simple. Her Oscar win did not immediately open the doors people assumed it would. She worked — film after film, some good, many forgettable, a career that continued without quite becoming what the award had implied it might. The industry had a talent for doing exactly that. 

For conferring the highest recognition and then not quite following through.

Then, in 2001, Todd Field made a film called In the Bedroom. It was quiet and devastating — a drama about grief and the specific violence of loss in a small Maine town. Marisa Tomei played Natalie Strout, a woman at the centre of an unravelling. It was nothing like Mona Lisa Vito. There was no courtroom, no comedy, no cocktail dress.

She was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress.

It was her second nomination. The first had not been a mistake.

Then, in 2008, Darren Aronofsky made The Wrestler. 

He cast Mickey Rourke as a washed-up professional wrestler trying to find his way back. He cast Marisa Tomei as Cassidy — a stripper navigating the particular arithmetic of that work, the performance of warmth with the wall behind it, the loneliness underneath. The performance was raw and precise and completely different again from anything she had done before.

She was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress.

Her third nomination.

Three films. Three completely different registers. 

Three times the Academy looked at the work and said: this was exceptional.

The rumour about Jack Palance never died entirely. It still circulates, still told with confidence by people who are certain it happened. The certificate from March 29, 1993 says otherwise. So does everything that came after.

She didn’t win it by accident.

She won it because she was that good.

The gasp in the room was the only thing that got it wrong.

posts.text:
It's crazy how wrong the New York Times-reading crowd has it on AI, China, and Nvidia:

1. China and the CCP do NOT WANT Nvidia chips. Chinese companies do, the Chinese government does not (similar to how there are no Chinese cars in the US — you'd love a BYD car!). Proof? Look here:
https://t.co/MEOhvwBzYX

2. The world is so interconnected that you don't need "chips" in your physical control to use them. It's why datacenters are all over the world and can (and do!) handle workloads from all over the world. It's a combinatorial nightmare. Until last week, a Brazilian company could buy chips from the US (totally legal under US law) and then let an Iranian company run workloads on those chips (totally legal under Brazilian and Iranian law). The Department of Commerce just put out a new rule to close this (https://t.co/DvflNJmX44): chips to Brazil now need a license, and so does any datacenter selling serious compute to companies from China, Iran, etc. But look at how it works. Enforcement runs on know-your-customer paperwork, the datacenter test only kicks in above roughly 750 H100s' worth of compute, and the only leverage is withholding FUTURE chips. Laws change; adversaries and allies change; chips that have already shipped stay shipped. Can't yank back the old chips!

3. The best corporate governance means prioritizing SHAREHOLDERS, which is quite hard to do given the principal-agent problem. It's not about following the Ten Commandments or some moral code. "Bad corporate governance" and a corporation worth $4T seems preferable to "good corporate governance" and one worth $0. Shareholders are electing how they want the corporation to be governed in real time. This is great!

4. "Doesn't this teach a bad lesson?" Possibly! But again this is part of the shareholder calculus; if nobody wants to work at Nvidia because of this, presumably the company and its shareholders will suffer. Given the heroic "welcome back" from rank and file Nvidians, it seems many employees are quite happy. It’s clear shareholders overwhelmingly wanted Jensen back.

5. "Isn't it socialist to have the government intervene?" If an unproven spy narrative was hanging over the board's decision, the only party able to say whether there's a national security risk is…the US government! No politician should be able to "force" a company to hire or fire somebody (and what would those critical of Jensen's reinstatement say if it turns out his ousting was the result of government pressure?).

6. This isn't like nuclear. Follow that metaphor and you'll recall that there is "good" nuclear (power!) and "bad" nuclear (bombs!). But the metaphor breaks on the technology. Enriching uranium is a physical chokepoint: you have the centrifuges or you don't. Compute can be rented from anywhere (see #2), replaced with more of a worse chip, and gets cheaper every time algorithms improve (see DeepSeek). I've written (https://t.co/V20LDcLA1I) about why "who controls AI" matters so much: the model decides the answer to questions like "what happened in Beijing on June 4, 1989." Chips don't. But if the world's AI is built on the American stack (which, incidentally, is almost all made in Taiwan!), America keeps the leverage, the revenue that funds the next generation of companies, and the best shot at US companies (versus Chinese companies) being the dominant global AI platforms. My OPINION is that we are well served by having American goods be dominant across the world, including at our adversaries. Which is exactly why we should want them hooked: Beijing is blocking the chips (see #1) because it fears the dependence. Pepsi and Levi's arguably helped us beat the USSR as much as our military did. Other opinions might differ. But many opinions are based on a cartoon-like understanding of how chips and AI work, as if each Nvidia GPU is highly enriched uranium, without which our adversaries would simply…surrender.

SpaceX has agreed to forgo $738 million in U.S. federal broadband subsidies and instead provide free @Starlink hardware to eligible American households.

NTIA: "To ensure that no consumer at a Covered BSL is left behind, the provider (SpaceX) will serve the covered BSLs as this agreement provides. This includes providing customer premises equipment at no cost to new subscribers, so that households at covered BSL do not face the upfront equipment costs. Additionally, the provider’s broadband service will be subject to the same delivery timelines and performance testing requirements applicable to all recipients of BEAD funds."

Under the new agreement, SpaceX would:
• Provide free Starlink hardware to eligible households.
• Guarantee minimum download speeds of 100 Mbps and upload speeds of 20 Mbps.
• Offer a low-cost monthly internet plan.
• Commit to providing service for 10 years.
• Continue to comply with federal performance testing requirements.

The agreement will save American taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars while accelerating high-speed internet access in underserved rural communities.

In exchange, SpaceX would be exempt from most BEAD-related financial audits, procurement requirements and administrative reporting, while remaining subject to network performance testing.

And the impact goes far beyond connecting homes

In Zambia, Starlink has connected more than 600 healthcare facilities, helping medical workers access digital health systems, remote consultations and essential medical information

In Mozambique, over 300 schools have been connected, giving students and teachers access to online learning in rural communities

Across Africa, Starlink is helping connect:

• Rural homes and underserved communities
• Schools and healthcare facilities
• Farms, businesses and remote industries
• Emergency and disaster response teams
• Government services in hard-to-reach regions

For decades, connecting remote communities meant building expensive infrastructure, laying cables and extending networks over enormous distances

Starlink is changing that

A village, school or hospital no longer has to wait years for fiber infrastructure to reach it before getting access to high-speed internet

All it needs is a Starlink terminal, power and a clear view of the sky

That's what makes satellite connectivity so important for Africa's future

posts.text:
A 75-year-old grandmother helped have a man shot twice in the head in his own garage  all because a judge wouldn't let her daughter move the grandkids to another city. The man she had killed was the father of those children.

His name was Dan Markel, a 41-year-old Harvard graduate and law professor at Florida State  a scholar who literally studied the philosophy of punishment. On July 18, 2014, he pulled into his Tallahassee garage and a hired gunman shot him twice in the head, then sped off in a Toyota Prius.

For years it looked unsolvable. Then it unraveled. The gunman, Sigfredo Garcia, was paid through a woman who sat on the Adelson family's dental-practice payroll while doing no actual work. The driver admitted he got $35,000. Every thread led back to the same family  the family of Markel's ex-wife, Wendi Adelson.

Her brother Charlie, a periodontist, was convicted in 2023 of orchestrating the hit. And at the top of it sat the matriarch: Donna Adelson, who prosecutors said was consumed with rage that Markel was limiting her access to her grandchildren.

The night her son was convicted, Donna and her husband booked one-way tickets to Vietnam. They were arrested at the Miami airport. On a jailhouse call, she'd been recorded saying they were "looking for places where there's no extradition."

On September 4, 2025, a jury took just a few hours to convict her on every count. As the verdict was read, the 75-year-old grandmother broke down sobbing. Weeks later she was sentenced to life with no chance of parole.

A father of two is dead because his own family couldn't accept losing a custody fight. So is life in a cell enough for a grandmother who ordered a child's father executed  or does nothing ever truly balance that out?
